slides.say: Two fair dice, one blue and one red, are tossed. What is the probability that the number obtained on the blue die will be at least as large as the number obtained on the red die?

Fair dice is the exam's way of saying regular dice, where each of the six numbers is equally likely. And at least as large means bigger or equal, so a tie counts too. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with a table of all the cases, and then with an insight.

We haven't learned probability yet, so here's the little we need. A probability is the number of good results, out of all the results, when every result is equally likely. For example, the chance of a five on one die is one out of six, one sixth.
With two dice, each of the six red numbers can come with each of the six blue numbers. That's six times six, thirty-six pairs, and they're all equally likely.
How do we find the good pairs? The blue number we need depends on the red one. So let's make a table, with a row for each red number.
If the red shows one, every blue number is good. One, two, three, four, five or six, even the one, because equal is allowed. That's six good pairs.

In the language of probability, the chance of a red one is one sixth, and the chance of a good blue is six sixths. When both must happen, we multiply. One sixth times six sixths is six thirty-sixths. It's the same as counting, six good pairs out of thirty-six.

If the red shows two, the blue must be two, three, four, five or six. That's five good pairs. And so on. Red three gives four, red four gives three, red five gives two, and red six gives only one, a blue six.
These cases are linked with or. This one happens, or this one, or this one. With or, we add. Six plus five plus four plus three plus two plus one is twenty-one.
So the probability is twenty-one out of thirty-six. Both divide by three, so it's seven twelfths, and choice number four is our answer.
at: choice number four is our answer

slides: That was the mathematical way. It's long, because we listed every case. And it's not trivial. Many students don't get there at all.

slides.say: [pause] So far, we've met super-methods. In this question there's also an insight. What's an insight? An idea that belongs to one specific question. It's not a method you learn once and use again, because in another question it will be something completely different. These questions are rarer, but they're on the exam, so we'll practice them.
Here's the insight. Every one of the thirty-six pairs is one of three kinds. The red is higher, the blue is higher, or it's a tie, a double.
Two dice have six doubles. One and one, two and two, and so on up to six and six. Take them away, and thirty pairs are left.

Those thirty split equally. Why? The dice are the same, except for the color. Every pair where the red is higher has a twin where the blue is higher. Red five and blue two, swap them, and it's red two and blue five.
So in fifteen pairs the red is higher, and in fifteen the blue is higher.
Now, at least as large means ties count too. Fifteen pairs where the blue is higher, plus the six doubles, that's twenty-one out of thirty-six. Seven twelfths again, choice number four.
Careful here. Whoever says it's symmetric, so it's a half, forgets the ties, and marks choice number two. That's the trap.

So when do we look for an insight? There's no fixed sign, but here's a hint. When the long way means listing many cases, stop for a moment, and ask if something in the question is symmetric or special. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
